title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”
author: Connie Loizos
contentSnippet:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the booming AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.

The question now is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that pe

summary.tldr:
Nvidia’s board has initiated an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang following his admission of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed. U.S. officials have reportedly identified Alice Huang as a potential Chinese intelligence asset, raising concerns regarding the security of Nvidia’s proprietary technology and its compliance with U.S. export restrictions. While the board currently reports no evidence of compromised national security or company secrets, the situation has created a significant leadership crisis for the company, which serves as a central pillar of the global AI economy.

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, estimates Huang’s probability of retaining his position at 50-50. The challenge is compounded by Nvidia’s flat organizational structure—featuring approximately 60 direct reports to Huang—and the lack of a clear internal successor. Furthermore, Nvidia’s role as a primary financier for the AI sector, including investments in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave, and Nebius, alongside a $500 billion mobilization initiative involving firms like BlackRock and KKR, makes the company's stability critical to broader market health. Huang is scheduled to report earnings on November 17 and attend a closed-door briefing with three House chairmen on November 18.
takeaways: **Leadership Structure:** Nvidia lacks a traditional succession hierarchy, with Jensen Huang maintaining a flat management structure of approximately 60 direct reports.

**Financial Exposure:** Nvidia has committed to backstopping up to 25% of a $500 billion mobilization effort involving partners including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR.

**Megaspeed Allegations:** Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud firm, purchased approximately $2 billion in Nvidia chips, prompting scrutiny over potential re-exportation or remote access by Chinese entities.
**Governance Vulnerability:** Unlike many tech founders, Jensen Huang does not hold super-voting stock, making him more susceptible to removal by the board of directors.

**Regulatory Pressure:** Three U.S. House chairmen have requested a closed-door briefing with Huang scheduled for November 18, following reports that U.S. intelligence briefed President Trump on the situation a year ago.

title: Korea Advances Physical AI Across Industries With NVIDIA
author: NVIDIA Writers
contentSnippet: Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem. The country’s industry leaders are applying accelerated computing, AI and simulation to everything from semiconductor manufacturing to robotics and autonomous vehicles. These efforts are helping bring physical AI from development into real-world production. Samsung Advances Semiconductor Engineering With Accelerated Computing and AI Physics Samsung Electronics is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to advance semiconductor innovation through accelerated computing and AI physics. The work spans materials research, process development and device engineering. In technology computer-aided design, Samsung is working with NVIDIA cuISS and NVIDIA cuDSS to accelerate computations involving sparse linear systems. The collaboration also extends to GPU acceleration for process and optical simulations. In materials research, Samsung’s sMOL platform has run selected quantum chemical calculations up to 5x faster end to end with NVIDIA cuEST . Samsung is also exploring NVIDIA cuEquivariance to speed up tensor operations used in training and inference for atomistic AI models. Samsung is developing chip-scale thermal and mechanical analysis workflows with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo . In one AI homogenization case, combining AI-predicted effective material properties, coarser grids and GPU acceleration resulted in a roughly 1,600x speedup. Simulation time fell from about 18 hours for a fine-grid solve on a 32-core CPU to 41 seconds for a GPU-accelerated coarse-grid solve. Looking ahead, NVIDIA Agent Toolkit could connect these simulation tools and AI models, helping future engineering agents run analyses and compare design options. The work combines Kakao Mobility’s proprietary driving software and experience operating in Seoul’s Gangnam district with NVIDIA’s vehicle computing platform. Kakao Mobility plans to use NVIDIA Hyperion , a reference platform for vehicle sensors and compute, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. It also plans to use NVIDIA Halos to support safety across the development and validation of its auto

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA is deepening its integration into South Korea’s industrial sector, focusing on physical AI applications across semiconductor manufacturing and autonomous vehicle development. Samsung Electronics is leveraging NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack—including cuISS, cuDSS, cuEST, cuEquivariance, and PhysicsNeMo—to optimize semiconductor materials research, process development, and device engineering. These tools are being applied to accelerate complex computations, such as sparse linear systems and quantum chemical calculations, with specific workflows achieving performance gains of up to 5x in materials research and 1,600x in AI homogenization tasks.

In the automotive sector, Kakao Mobility is partnering with NVIDIA to develop a Level 4 autonomous driving system. The collaboration integrates Kakao’s proprietary software, refined through operations in Seoul’s Gangnam district, with NVIDIA’s Hyperion reference platform and DRIVE AGX Thor computing architecture. Kakao Mobility also intends to utilize NVIDIA Halos to manage safety validation throughout the development lifecycle of its autonomous vehicle technology.
takeaways: **Semiconductor Performance:** Samsung achieved a 1,600x speedup in AI homogenization, reducing simulation time from 18 hours on a 32-core CPU to 41 seconds on a GPU-accelerated system.
**Materials Research:** Samsung’s sMOL platform utilized NVIDIA cuEST to accelerate quantum chemical calculations by up to 5x.

**Autonomous Driving Hardware:** Kakao Mobility is adopting the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor platform and the NVIDIA Hyperion sensor/compute reference architecture for its Level 4 autonomous driving project.
**Future Engineering Workflows:** Samsung is exploring the use of the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit to connect simulation tools and AI models for autonomous engineering design analysis.

title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
author: Nicola Sessions
contentSnippet:
As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them.

Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows .

A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions.

AIM Intelligence , a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments.

On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea .

Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents.

Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell .

Related News AI Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA is expanding its AI agent infrastructure in the Korean market through the introduction of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, specifically featuring the OpenShell runtime. OpenShell provides a sandboxed execution environment with policy-based controls designed to manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions. Hyundai Motor Group is currently exploring the use of NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and OpenShell, while Korean security firm AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with OpenShell to combine runtime access controls with Starfort’s existing capabilities for detecting malicious instructions and data leakage. Potential applications for this integrated security stack include the public energy sector, industrial robotics, and general enterprise workflows.

Simultaneously, LG AI Research has opened API access for its K-EXAONE-2.5 model, which was developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets. A critical component of this development is the Nemotron-Personas-Korea dataset, an open resource containing 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas. These personas are grounded in official Korean statistics and are intended to provide model builders with localized training and evaluation data for specialized AI agents.
takeaways: **OpenShell Security:** A runtime environment featuring sandboxed execution and policy-based controls for governing autonomous agent actions and data access.
**AIM Intelligence Integration:** The Starfort platform is being integrated with OpenShell to provide a dual-layer defense against malicious instructions and data leakage.
**K-EXAONE-2.5 Availability:** LG AI Research has opened API access for the K-EXAONE-2.5 model, built using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets.
**Synthetic Data Resource:** Nemotron-Personas-Korea provides 7 million synthetic personas based on official Korean statistics to improve model grounding in local contexts.

title: From Chips to Skills, NVIDIA and Korea Expand Sovereign AI Collaboration
author: Jesse Clayton
contentSnippet:
NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security.

The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization.

Through Korea’s AI for All initiative, NVIDIA will collaborate with three selected consortia and four leading Korean foundation model builders, using NVIDIA Dynamo software to optimize and scale AI inference.

In addition, NVIDIA today announced a collaboration with SK Telecom and Rebellions, supported by MSIT, to advance sovereign AI infrastructure for Korean models and workloads with NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. Read more in the press release .

Related News AI Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA and South Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) have formalized an expanded partnership to bolster the nation's sovereign AI ecosystem. The collaboration spans the entire AI stack, including semiconductor development, data center infrastructure, workforce training, and startup support. A primary objective is to integrate Korean NPU and XPU manufacturers into the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, facilitating deeper technical interoperability between domestic hardware and NVIDIA’s high-performance computing architecture.

Under the 'AI for All' initiative, NVIDIA is partnering with three consortia and four Korean foundation model developers to deploy NVIDIA Dynamo software for optimizing and scaling AI inference workloads. Furthermore, NVIDIA, SK Telecom, and Rebellions have launched a joint effort to build sovereign AI infrastructure specifically tailored for Korean-language models and local workloads, utilizing NVLink Fusion to enhance performance. The collaboration also includes a commitment to human capital development through NVIDIA-led certification programs, technical seminars, and hackathons designed to maximize GPU utilization across the Korean tech sector.
takeaways: **Hardware Integration:** Korean NPU and XPU companies are being positioned to participate in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem.
**Software Optimization:** NVIDIA Dynamo software will be utilized by four Korean foundation model builders and three consortia to scale AI inference.
**Strategic Partnership:** NVIDIA, SK Telecom, and Rebellions are collaborating on sovereign AI infrastructure supported by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT).
**Workforce Development:** The initiative includes NVIDIA-led training, certification programs, and hackathons to increase domestic GPU utilization expertise.

title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
author: Tanat Tonguthaisri
contentSnippet:
Authors: Tanat Tonguthaisri

Abstract: This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology. Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.

Notes: 2026 proofread digital edition of the August 2003 Master of Engineering thesis, RMIT University

summary.tldr:
Tanat Tonguthaisri’s 2003 Master of Engineering thesis from RMIT University, re-released in a 2026 digital edition, details the design, development, and validation of a prototype Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) system for academic advisement. The research addresses the inefficiencies of traditional higher education advising by applying CBR methodology—a problem-solving technique that utilizes past experiences to inform current decisions—to the specific domain of student course planning and academic guidance.

The thesis posits that while CBR has been successfully deployed across various human problem-solving domains over the preceding decade, its application to academic advising remained largely unexplored. The prototype system is intended to function as a supplemental tool for human advisors, with the long-term objective of potentially automating the advising process entirely. The work serves as a foundational exploration into how expert systems can mitigate the time-intensive nature of institutional academic support.
takeaways: **Research Origin:** Master of Engineering thesis authored by Tanat Tonguthaisri at RMIT University, originally published in August 2003.
**Core Methodology:** Application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) expert systems to the domain of higher education academic advising.
**System Objective:** Development of a prototype recommender system designed to supplement or eventually replace human academic advisors.
**Problem Domain:** Addressing the time-consuming nature of academic advising and the lack of existing expert system implementations in this specific field.

title: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
author: Binze Li, Zihuan Zhang, Seokhyun Baek, Gillian K. Hadfield, Tianmin Shu
contentSnippet:
Authors: Binze Li , Zihuan Zhang , Seokhyun Baek , Gillian K. Hadfield , Tianmin Shu

Abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.

summary.tldr:
Binze Li, Zihuan Zhang, Seokhyun Baek, Gillian K. Hadfield, and Tianmin Shu introduced NormGym, an interactive benchmark designed to evaluate normative competence—the capacity of agents to infer hidden, arbitrary social norms from interaction and adjust their behavior accordingly in multi-agent communities.

NormGym evaluates whether agents can distinguish between what is possible versus what is permitted, deduce unknown rules from observed behaviors and sanctions, and apply those rules to novel situations while pursuing their primary tasks. Testing various large language model (LLM) agents on the benchmark reveals that the strongest evaluated model achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of only 55.3%.

Further analysis indicates that while models can occasionally adjust their actions after being directly sanctioned, they largely fail to deduce underlying norms by observing the behavior of and sanctions directed at other agents. The authors also found that standard model fine-tuning may be insufficient to resolve these deficits, demonstrating that current LLMs lack a robust, transferable capability for normative knowledge acquisition via social interaction.
takeaways: **Core Benchmark:** NormGym is an interactive benchmark evaluating normative competence by requiring newcomer agents to infer hidden, arbitrary norms within multi-agent communities.
**Performance Metric:** The strongest evaluated large language model achieved a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3% on NormGym.

**Behavioral Limitation:** Evaluated models can sometimes revise their behavior following direct sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to infer norms from observing other agents' behaviors and sanctions.
**Mitigation Finding:** The study indicates that standard model fine-tuning may be insufficient to fix the lack of robust, transferable normative competence in current LLMs.

title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
author: Humza Akhtar, Rami Pinto
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced a novel framework for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification (MCIC) that integrates unstructured data—specifically customer feedback—into traditional inventory management models. Detailed in arXiv:2611.08626v1, the approach moves beyond standard ABC analysis and existing MCIC methods, which typically rely exclusively on structured quantitative metrics like annual dollar usage. By utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform feature extraction, the authors convert qualitative customer reviews into quantitative vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria.

The methodology incorporates these LLM-derived features into the Hadi-Vencheh model, a mathematical framework for multi-criteria decision-making. Experimental results indicate that the inclusion of customer sentiment signals leads to measurable reclassification effects, suggesting that inventory prioritization can be significantly improved by capturing unstructured operational data. This approach addresses the underutilization of qualitative feedback in e-commerce supply chains, providing a bridge between natural language processing and traditional inventory optimization techniques.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Utilizes LLM-based feature extraction to convert unstructured customer reviews into quantitative vector embeddings.
**Framework Integration:** Incorporates enriched feature sets into the Hadi-Vencheh model for multi-criteria inventory classification.
**Performance:** Demonstrates measurable reclassification effects in inventory prioritization when sentiment signals are integrated.
**Scope:** Targets the limitation of traditional ABC analysis and existing MCIC methods that ignore unstructured supply chain data.

title: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
author: Hannah Guan, Yilun Du
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), a novel test-time compute strategy designed to improve LLM reasoning by replacing traditional absolute scoring with comparative, multi-aspect evaluation. Instead of judging candidates in isolation, APT organizes candidate solutions into a single-elimination tournament where each matchup is decided by a committee of off-the-shelf aspect verifiers. By breaking down complex evaluations into specific, natural language-defined criteria, the method allows for granular preference alignment without requiring model retraining or fine-tuning.

In empirical testing across five domains and three distinct generator LLMs, APT outperformed established baselines including binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency, and reward model verification. The researchers observed the most significant performance gains in open-ended tasks, noting that the combination of both pairwise comparison and aspect-specific verification is essential for success. Because the system relies on natural language prompts for aspect definition, it offers high portability, allowing users to steer model selection toward specific properties by simply updating the verifier prompts.
takeaways: **Methodology:** APT utilizes a single-elimination tournament structure where winners are determined by a vote across multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers.
**Performance:** The method demonstrated superior results compared to binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency, and reward model verification, particularly in open-ended reasoning tasks.
**Flexibility:** APT requires no training or fine-tuning, enabling domain transfer and preference steering through simple natural language prompt modification.

**Architecture:** The system mandates both pairwise comparison and aspect-specific evaluation, as neither binary approval nor generic pairwise judges matched the performance of the combined APT approach.

title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
author: Nima Vahdat, Pashootan Vaezipoor
contentSnippet:
Authors: Nima Vahdat , Pashootan Vaezipoor

Abstract: LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge. We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query. Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.

Notes: 12 pages. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)

summary.tldr:
Nima Vahdat and Pashootan Vaezipoor have introduced 'Forge Decision Context' (forge_dc), a system designed to enable persistent behavioral learning in LLM agents. Unlike existing memory architectures that focus on static facts, entities, or conversational history, forge_dc captures procedural knowledge from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures. It compiles these signals into imperative 'RULE' directives, which are then injected into the agent's decision-making process at the specific points where they are relevant, preventing the common issue of users needing to repeat corrections across sessions.

The authors evaluated forge_dc using 'DC-Bench,' a new benchmark consisting of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions derived from real agent traces in a deterministic, mocked-tool environment. In testing, forge_dc achieved a 95% compliance rate, significantly outperforming the 55% compliance rate observed with naive retrieval methods. Furthermore, the system is highly efficient, requiring approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query compared to baseline approaches. The research concludes that the effectiveness of persistent behavioral learning hinges on three design pillars: the representation of memory as explicit directives, the activation of that memory, and the precise placement of directives within the agent's decision loop.
takeaways: **System Architecture:** forge_dc converts behavioral signals from corrections and failures into imperative RULE directives for targeted injection.
**Benchmark Performance:** The system achieved 95% compliance on DC-Bench, compared to 55% for naive retrieval methods.
**Efficiency Metric:** forge_dc reduces token overhead by approximately 10x per query compared to predecessor approaches.
**Benchmark Scope:** DC-Bench comprises 71 distinct scenarios covering nine behavioral dimensions based on real-world agent execution traces.
**Academic Context:** The 12-page paper was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM).

title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
author: Chris von Csefalvay, Pranav Doma, Achyuthan Unni Krishnan, Tam\'as F\"oldi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced IWIBench, a systematic evaluation framework designed to measure the efficacy of 'intra-weight injection'—a technique where a large editor model modifies the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) without using gradients. The benchmark tests models across ten distinct text-editing objectives, ranging from lexical association changes to output format enforcement. Editors are constrained by a fixed budget for rollouts and limited to four specific tools for reading and writing tensor data, with performance validated in a clean environment against an unmodified baseline.

Performance analysis reveals a significant capability gap, with Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol emerging as the top-performing models. The study notes that this capability appears to be a recent development, as it is largely absent in GPT-5.6 Sol. Task difficulty varies drastically: while alias acquisition and recoding are achievable, structured response and answer-length control remain largely resistant to current editing methods. The lack of correlation between success in different task families suggests that intra-weight injection capabilities are currently uneven and highly specialized.
takeaways: **Benchmark Target:** Gemma 3 4B IT serves as the primary target model for weight-editing experiments.
**Top Performers:** Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol significantly outperform other evaluated models in weight-injection tasks.
**Task Difficulty:** Alias acquisition and recoding are the most successful task categories, while structured response and answer-length control remain largely unsolved.
**Capability Evolution:** The ability to perform gradient-free weight editing is a recent emergence, absent in the GPT-5.6 Sol model.
**Constraint Framework:** Editors are restricted to four specific weight-reading/writing tools and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts.

title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
author: Ryan Magnuson, Ellie Kitanidis, Ariel Lee
contentSnippet:
Authors: Ryan Magnuson , Ellie Kitanidis , Ariel Lee

Abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.

Notes: Accepted, NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development"

summary.tldr:
In a study accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 workshop 'Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development,' researchers Ryan Magnuson, Ellie Kitanidis, and Ariel Lee investigate whether interactive debuggers provide a performance advantage over traditional bash-based edit-execute-observe loops for coding agents. By isolating the debugger as a distinct tool within a fixed scaffold, the authors evaluated agents on all 500 instances of the SWE-bench Verified benchmark. The study utilized two large language models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, conducting three independent runs per configuration to assess the efficacy of debugger-only versus bash-only architectures.

To rigorously evaluate these interfaces, the authors introduced 'pass$_X$@$k$', a cross-agent metric designed to estimate the probability that at least one of $k$ agents succeeds, effectively distinguishing between genuine tool complementarity and stochastic run-to-run variance. The results indicate that the performance differences observed between bash and debugger agents are primarily driven by variance rather than tool-specific capabilities. Across both models, the researchers found that two independent bash rollouts consistently outperformed the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout, suggesting that current debugger interfaces do not provide a reliable advantage over standard shell-based debugging tools.
takeaways: **Methodology:** Evaluated debugger-only versus bash-only agents across all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances.
**Models Tested:** Used GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B with three independent runs per configuration.
**Metric Innovation:** Introduced pass$_X$@$k$, an unbiased estimator for calculating the probability of success across multiple agent rollouts.
**Key Finding:** Two bash rollouts outperformed a combined bash-plus-debugger approach, indicating that observed performance gaps are largely due to stochastic variance.

title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
author: Selim Aktas, Yusuf Erdem Erdem, Ahmed Zeer, Himmet Toprak Kesgin, Muzaffer Kaan Yuce, Mehmet Fatih Amasyali
contentSnippet:
Authors: Selim Aktas , Yusuf Erdem Erdem , Ahmed Zeer , Himmet Toprak Kesgin , Muzaffer Kaan Yuce , Mehmet Fatih Amasyali

Abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.

summary.tldr:
ChainFlow is a novel speculative decoding framework developed by Selim Aktas and colleagues that utilizes flow matching conditioned on target model hidden states to accelerate LLM inference. Unlike traditional autoregressive drafters that suffer from linear cost scaling or diffusion-based drafters that struggle with inter-token dependencies, ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport process requiring only one or two flow steps. The architecture employs a variational autoencoder (VAE) to compress hidden states, ensuring that drafting overhead remains minimal regardless of target model size, while integrated feedback heads explicitly model inter-token dependencies to improve prediction accuracy.

In performance evaluations using Qwen3.5 models, ChainFlow demonstrated significant speedup advantages over existing state-of-the-art methods. When compared at equivalent drafter sizes and training data volumes, ChainFlow outperformed EAGLE-3 by 39% and DFlash by 11% within the vLLM inference engine. The framework also incorporates tree-based drafting to increase token acceptance rates and shows robust performance gains when adapted sequentially to new languages. The authors have released the source code and pre-trained drafter models to the public.
takeaways: **Architecture:** Employs a flow-matching paradigm conditioned on target hidden states, requiring only 1-2 steps for token generation.
**Efficiency:** Uses a VAE for state compression, decoupling drafting cost from target model size.
**Performance:** Achieves 39% higher speedup than EAGLE-3 and 11% over DFlash on Qwen3.5 models within vLLM.
**Methodology:** Integrates lightweight feedback heads to restore inter-token dependencies and utilizes tree drafting to boost acceptance rates.
**Availability:** Code and pre-trained drafter models are open-sourced.

title: Transporting the Past: An Optimal Transport View of Backtracking Counterfactuals
author: Zhangyi Liu, Pouria Fatemi, Suvrit Sra
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study backtracking counterfactual inference for Structural Causal Models (SCMs) through the lens of optimal transport. In SCMs, a factual observation generally induces a posterior distribution over exogenous variables, making counterfactual inference inherently distributional. We introduce two complementary frameworks that transport this posterior onto the set of exogenous configurations satisfying a desired counterfactual query. The first constructs a natural pointwise projection and is suitable when the transported exogenous distribution can be used directly. The second enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables, so that the transported variables remain interpretable as genuine exogenous noises of the same SCM. We show that both frameworks are consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle, and we propose marginal, penalty-based, and hard-constrained solvers for finite-posterior settings. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the geometry of the problem and reveal trade-offs among transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.

title: Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine
author: Xindan Zhang, Fei Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.

title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
author: Emilly Pitman de Castro, Vanessa Silva, Gustavo Kanno, Marcus Santos, Bruno Ferraz do Amaral, Marcelo Nogueira, Lucas Francisco Pellicer, Lucas Lanaro, Pedro Augusto Luiz, Jo\~ao Renato Ribeiro Manesco, Giovanni Carbinatti, Isabela de Lima Santos, Lucas Oliveira Jeronymo, Jeison Fappi, Raul Rotilli Aguirre, Fabio Andr\'e Frantz, Renata De Paris, Fabiana Marucci, Lohan Silva, Vinicius Diniz Reolon, Wandemberg Gibaut
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues. In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.

title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
author: Alexander Kastius
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.

title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
author: Doniyorkhon Obidov, Honggang Yu, Xiaolong Guo, Kaichen Yang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.

title: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
author: Liting Huang, Huizhi Liang, Yi Lei, Xingjun Ma, Varun Ojha
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge attacks on Large Language Models, such as manipulating fact-checking judgments, pose significant risks to AI reliability. Existing approaches -- adversarial suffix/template injection and single-agent self-reflection -- lack robustness across diverse defenses and are prone to confirmation bias and costly trial-and-error, respectively. We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounded in human debate structure and rhetorical style, enabling agents to generate adversarial passages that are semantically coherent, rhetorically effective, and resistant to early confirmation bias. D2D formalizes the adversarial process as an evolutionary game in which agents adaptively evolve their rhetorical strategies (Logos, Pathos, Ethos) through competition. To manage the intractably large LLM output space, we decouple agent behavior into a strategic layer, which selects a rhetorical action from a compact strategy space via evolutionary-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer, where the LLM produces a concrete passage conditioned on that strategy and the debate context. On four fact-checking benchmarks (FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact), D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses.

title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
author: Marvin Danig (Achiral Research)
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08779v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments
author: Stephen Peng, Vineet Jagadeesan Nair, Noah Broestl, Anne Friederike Kleppe, Steven Mills, Adi Zolotov
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.

title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years
author: Jesus S. Aguilar-Ruiz
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08799v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.

title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
author: Parth Illendula, Garik Livingston, Zain Shamsi, Ravi Srinivasan, Alex Liu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08811v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.

title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
author: Mark Heimann, Katherine Taylor, Bruno Jacob
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.

title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates
author: Vineet Jagadeesan Nair, Stephen Peng, Arun Ravindran
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Equivalent encodings of an optimization problem can produce different learned predictions. Interpreting these differences requires accounting for numerical error and multiple optima. We construct metamorphic tests for optimization solver surrogates with explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment, and numerical thresholds. Reference-solver agreement and independent constraint checks determine which sampled pairs enter the audit. We study alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), and maximum independent set (MIS). Across five grids, GridSFM-Open violates each of 13 relations on at least one grid, and 12 by more than twice the threshold. Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training. Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid. In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities. Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws. Post hoc normalization within connected components removes these violations on the tested graphs. These findings support reporting metamorphic consistency alongside optimality, feasibility, and accuracy, and validating repair quality separately from consistency.

takeaways: Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training.
Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid.
In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities.
Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws.

title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
author: Stepan Epifantsev, Anna Antipova, Oleg Chernikov, Leon Strelkov, Alexey Dontsov
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
author: Abhinav Arun, Jayita Bhattacharyya, Fabrizio Dimino, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.

title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
author: Laya Iyer, Sanmi Koyejo, Chen Shani
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings. We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.

title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
author: Michelle Morgenstern, Julia Witte Zimmerman, Tabia Tanzin Prama, Kristine Harootunian, June Clark, Bryn Loftness, Calla Beauregard, Juniper Lovato
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
author: Taikun Chen, Yue Zhang, Wei Qian, Hui Fang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at https://github.com/taikunudel/RL-ATTACK.

title: Structuring Survey Histories for LLM Digital Twins: A Controlled Study of Background, Decision Procedure, and Evaluation Profiles
author: Iris Ye, Tianze Deng, Ozan Candogan
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based digital twins aim to predict how individuals would respond in new settings from representations of their prior responses. Existing evidence that compression of survey histories need not reduce predictive accuracy suggests that representation structure, rather than information volume alone, may be an important design choice. We study BDE, a fixed representation that organizes each respondent's survey history into Background, Decision procedure, and Evaluation. We evaluate it on Twin-2K-500 (Toubia et al., 2025) by predicting each respondent's held-out answers on 17 tasks. In a paired evaluation with 100 respondents, a fully inferred BDE profile improves overall accuracy over the raw survey transcript by 1.27 percentage points (pp) on gpt-5.4-nano (p < 0.01) and 1.19 pp on gpt-5.4-mini (p < 0.001). Three analyses then examine the schema, extraction depth, and component composition. Against a length-matched free-form profile written from the same transcript by the same extractor, BDE improves pricing accuracy on both simulators (2.15 pp on nano, p < 0.01; 1.38 pp on mini, p < 0.05), while its overall advantage is significant only on nano (1.05 pp, p < 0.05). Allowing deeper inference during extraction yields no statistically significant gain on either simulator. By contrast, adding Evaluation to a Background--Decision procedure profile improves overall accuracy by 1.44 pp on nano (p < 0.001) and 1.22 pp on mini (p < 0.001). These results indicate that the advantage over raw transcripts is not explained by compression or length alone, and attribute it primarily to profile composition rather than deeper extraction.

title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
author: Mehmet Murat Albayrako\u{g}lu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.

title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
author: Stephen Peng, Vineet Jagadeesan Nair, Noah Broestl, Anne Friederike Kleppe, Steven Mills, Adi Zolotov
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
author: Pranjal Srivastava
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.08892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. Next-token identities and a categorical simulation isolate decoding and sampling effects; the crossing order remains empirical. Fine-tuning on human text can produce the same split while likelihood improves, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood across the tested settings. We recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets with an independent quality measure.
